A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RDB-PFN study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Existing proofs and experiments can be matched despite appendix renumbering and added analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on 19 relational prediction tasks and 23 single-table datasets, including model comparisons, pretraining comparisons and inference timing.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds stronger-baseline comparisons, PR-AUC evaluation, adaptation experiments, context scaling and component ablations.

M1.justification: Section 5.1.3 changes the specified feature decoder from Gaussian/Softmax sampling to clipping/normalization and discretization/binning. Appendix D.2 adds optional gradient adaptation and chunked-support probability averaging. The three-stage prior and main Transformer architecture remain; revised parameter counts alone do not establish an architecture replacement.

E1.justification: Tables 1–3 retain the same 19 binary relational tasks from 13 databases and 23 single-table datasets. The additional experiments reuse this coverage, changing adaptation procedures, metrics, support sizes or component configurations without introducing new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: Figure 6a and Tables 6–10 add XGBoost-Tuned and AutoGluon-Best alongside the retained comparators; AutoGluon-Medium corresponds to v1's AutoGluon. Table 17 additionally evaluates fine-tuned TabPFNv2.5 against the adapted RDB-PFN variants. Griffin remains a reported reference, while RT remains discussion-only.

E3.justification: Appendix D introduces PR-AUC evaluation, target-task and cross-dataset fine-tuning, effective support sizes up to 8192, component ablations trained with 20k RDBs, and DFS sensitivity protocols. RDB-PFN fine-tuning uses 1000 steps with 1024 samples per step. Appendix C.2.2 also removes Sum from the specified DFS aggregation set. These extend the retained main few-shot protocol substantially.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's single-table-only comparison and qualitative visualizations, v2 directly ablates schema generation, link generation, temporal signals, locality, model capacity and attention ordering. It also tests DFS depth and aggregation choices, alternative metrics, adaptation and larger support sets (Appendix D, Figures 8–10 and Table 4).

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten random seeds for relational evaluation, mean and standard-deviation reporting, and ten repeated single-table trials in Appendix A.3. Shaded uncertainty bands already appear in v1. v2 introduces no new stated uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test or increased run count.

E6.justification: All matched entries in the original ROC-AUC and single-table result tables remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive results for stronger baselines, PR-AUC, adaptation, support scaling and ablations; Table 17 reports average ROC-AUC of 0.7342 for target-task fine-tuning and 0.7261 for cross-task fine-tuning under those new conditions. Efficiency reporting also changes, including RDB-PFN's parameter count from 2.64M to 0.7M while retaining its 34-second timing.

T1.justification: The completeness and universality definitions, assumptions, theorems and proofs are unchanged after matching v1 Appendix D to v2 Appendix E. Assumption 4.2 replaces generic value/rest notation with explicit attribute and conditioning notation without changing the locality condition.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central claims: synthetic relational pretraining, universality within an assumption-defined family, gradient-free in-context learning and strong relational few-shot performance with efficient inference. The revised conclusion and additional experiments do not redefine the main contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 now attributes much of the speed advantage to avoiding default ensembling. Section 6.3 treats single-table performance as a transfer and scope check instead of using the specialization gap to confirm the source of relational superiority. Appendix D adds interpretations of component importance, DFS sensitivity and adaptation/runtime trade-offs, while Section 7 explicitly discusses the binary, global-support and DFS applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies Kaiming-uniform initialization for learnable attention projections, running DFS before uniform row sampling, variable training/test ratios, the exact TabPFNv2.5 checkpoint, and budgets for additional experiments. These improve documentation; the principal architecture hyperparameters, optimizer, hardware, pretraining corpus composition and code-access information remain.

R1.justification: The bibliography is unchanged. Sections 6.1 and B.3 refine positioning relative to Griffin and RT by explicitly treating them as contextual relational references and distinguishing RT's local graph-conditioned label access from RDB-PFN's fixed global support. The broader positioning against real-data pretraining and privacy-oriented generators remains.

P1.justification: Targeted paragraph rewrites clarify assumptions, attention terminology, efficiency and transfer interpretations, and remove duplicated implementation prose. Section 7 becomes Conclusion and Limitations, and a new experimental Appendix D precedes the retained, renumbered proof and raw-results appendices. The main narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with revised resource values and axis labels; Figure 6 becomes a two-panel baseline comparison. New Figures 8–10 display PR-AUC, adaptation, context scaling and ablations. Table 4 and Tables 12–30 add substantial new displays, while existing relational result tables gain comparator rows. These exceed simple relocation or renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny of the central design choices through component and backbone ablations, DFS sensitivity, stronger baselines and PR-AUC checks, addressing important gaps in v1's evidence. Clearer protocol boundaries and more accurate speedup summaries also improve interpretation. The reduced 20k-RDB ablation budget limits conclusions about the full training pipeline, but the added controls and explicit limitations provide a substantial overall quality gain.
